The Variable sunbird (Cinnyris venustus) is a small nectivorous passerine of the family Nectariniidae, inhabiting a broad range of Afrotropical habitats from lowland forests to montane scrublands. Eggs incubated at 33 °C [T = 33 °C] typically hatch after 14 days [ab = 14 days], a duration consistent with incubation periods reported for other Afrotropical nectarinids of comparable body size. Upon hatching, the altricial nestlings emerge with a wet body mass of just 0.99 grams [Ww0 = 0.99 grams], a remarkably low initial mass that underscores the extreme altriciality of this species and the substantial energetic investment required from both parents during subsequent brooding and provisioning. The intense parental care drives rapid somatic growth; under the elevated metabolic conditions sustained by active heat production at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the young fledge after 18 days since birth [tx = 18 days since birth], acquiring flight feathers and leaving the nest at a stage still reliant on parental guidance for a further period.

Females of Cinnyris venustus attain a maximum adult wet body mass of 6.5 grams [Wwi = 6.5 grams], whereas males reach a slightly larger adult size of 7 grams [Wwi = 7 grams], a modest sexual size dimorphism typical of sunbird species where males engage in aerial displays and territorial defense. This size difference may influence the energetic demands of reproduction, as the larger males contribute more heavily to nest defense while females bear the primary costs of egg production and incubation. Both sexes reach sexual maturity at 54 days since birth [tp = 54 days since birth] when maintained at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], a relatively rapid maturation that permits early breeding in the first year of life, provided food resources are abundant and territory acquisition is successful. After reaching reproductive maturity, first broods typically appear at 365 days since birth [tR = 365 days since birth] under the same thermal regime, indicating a delay between physiological readiness and the actual initiation of reproductive effort, likely linked to seasonal constraints and the need to establish a stable breeding territory before attempting to rear young at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C].

The maximum reproductive rate of this species is expressed through a modest clutch size of 1 to 3 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 1 to 3 eggs per clutch], with females typically raising two broods per year [F_R_i = two broods per year] when conditions are favorable. This combination of small clutch size and high brood frequency is a common life-history strategy among tropical passerines, where nest predation is high but the extended breeding season allows multiple nesting attempts within a single year. Each brood requires substantial investment from both parents, with nestlings growing rapidly from their initial 0.99 grams [Ww0 = 0.99 grams] to near-fledging mass over approximately 18 days of intensive provisioning. The energetic cost of this growth is considerable, and the high brood frequency may be partially offset by the relatively short incubation period of 14 days at 33 °C [T = 33 °C], which reduces the total time each nest is exposed to predators.

Basal oxygen consumption in Cinnyris venustus reaches 25 milliliters per hour [JOi = 25 milliliters per hour] when measured at the species' typical active body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], a value that reflects the elevated metabolic demands of a small endotherm with a high surface-area-to-volume ratio and a nectarivorous diet requiring frequent feeding bouts. This resting metabolic rate is consistent with the general allometric relationship for sunbirds, although it sits at the higher end of the range for a bird of this body mass, possibly due to the energetic costs of hovering flight during foraging. The maximum lifespan recorded for this species in the wild is approximately 3869 days [am = approximately 3869 days], or just over 10.6 years, as determined from long-term mark-recapture studies conducted on populations in East African montane forests at an ambient temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. Such longevity is notable for a bird weighing only 7 grams in males, as small body size is generally correlated with higher mortality rates and shorter lifespans across passerine taxa.

The life-history of the Variable sunbird is thus characterized by a rapid early development, with eggs hatching after 14 days at 33 °C and nestlings reaching independence after a brief fledging period of 18 days, followed by a relatively early puberty at 54 days and first reproduction deferred until 365 days under the thermal regime of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This appears to be an adaptive strategy that balances high predation risk by compressing early life stages, while still allowing individuals to achieve a potentially long adult lifespan. The adult body mass of females at 6.5 grams and males at 7 grams supports a high metabolic rate that fuels demanding foraging and breeding activities, while repeated production of small clutches of 1 to 3 eggs twice per year ensures sufficient recruitment despite heavy nest losses. The species' success across a diversity of African habitats is a testament to the efficiency of this compact, energetically expensive life cycle.
